name: Sarah Chen
chief_complaint: Difficulty breathing and facial swelling after eating cashew nuts
opening_statement: I was eating at a restaurant about 15 minutes ago and had some cashew nuts. Within a few minutes my lips started tingling, then my face swelled up. Now I'm having trouble breathing and I feel dizzy.

socrates.radiation: Spreading from initial areas to entire body

rag_citation.quote: Cutaneous manifestations in anaphylaxis include urticaria (hives), angioedema, and flushing - present in 80-90% of cases
Angioedema involving lips, tongue, or upper airway is a critical feature of anaphylaxis requiring immediate adrenaline

socrates.character: Expiratory wheeze, shortness of breath, 'tight chest'

rag_citation.quote: Respiratory symptoms in anaphylaxis include wheeze, dyspnea, stridor, and upper airway obstruction - indicating severe reaction
Cardiovascular collapse (hypotension, syncope) indicates life-threatening anaphylaxis requiring immediate intervention

past_medical_history: Known cashew nut allergy (diagnosed age 12 after previous mild reaction)
medications: Salbutamol 100mcg PRN (asthma reliever - last used 2 weeks ago)
allergies: Cashew nuts (known), tree nuts (suspected - avoids all nuts)
family_history: Mother has allergic rhinitis, no family history of anaphylaxis

social_history.alcohol: Social drinker (2-3 standard drinks per week)

drsabcd_assessment.danger: No immediate danger in ED resuscitation bay
drsabcd_assessment.send_for_help: Resuscitation team alerted, senior ED physician present
drsabcd_assessment.airway: Patent but stridor audible - upper airway compromise
drsabcd_assessment.breathing: Tachypneic (RR 32/min), bilateral wheeze, SpO2 88% room air

vitals.spo2: 88% on room air → 94% on 15L/min non-rebreather mask

examination_findings.general: Distressed, anxious, using accessory muscles of respiration
examination_findings.skin: Widespread urticarial rash (raised red welts), facial angioedema (lip/periorbital swelling)
examination_findings.cardiovascular: Tachycardic, hypotensive, weak peripheral pulses, capillary refill 3 seconds
examination_findings.respiratory: Bilateral expiratory wheeze, stridor on inspiration, trachea central, chest expansion equal
examination_findings.neurological: Alert, oriented to time/place/person, no focal neurology

expected_management: IMMEDIATE TIME-CRITICAL MANAGEMENT:
1. Adrenaline 1:1000 (1mg/mL) 0.5mg (0.5mL) IM anterolateral thigh STAT - FIRST-LINE TREATMENT
- Repeat every 5-15 minutes if no improvement or recurrence of symptoms
2. High-flow oxygen 15L/min via non-rebreather mask (target SpO2 >94%)
3. IV access - two large-bore cannulas (16G or 18G)
4. Rapid IV fluid resuscitation - 1L 0.9% NaCl bolus (20-30mL/kg)
5. Position patient supine with legs elevated (unless airway/breathing compromise - then semi-recumbent)
SECONDARY MANAGEMENT:
6. Hydrocortisone 200mg IV (or prednisolone 50mg PO) - prevents biphasic reaction
7. Chlorphenamine 10mg IV (or promethazine 25mg IV) - antihistamine
8. Salbutamol 5mg nebulized (for bronchospasm - patient has asthma)
MONITORING:
9. Continuous cardiac monitoring, pulse oximetry
10. BP q5min initially, then q15min when stable
11. Observe for 4-6 hours minimum (biphasic reaction risk - occurs in 20% of cases)
DISCHARGE PLANNING:
12. Prescribe EpiPen (adrenaline auto-injector 0.3mg) x2
13. Provide anaphylaxis action plan (ASCIA guidelines)
14. Educate on EpiPen use, allergen avoidance
15. Refer to immunology/allergy clinic for allergen testing and follow-up
16. Medical alert bracelet recommendation
17. Advise to avoid all tree nuts (cross-reactivity risk)

critical_errors.error: Delayed adrenaline administration (adrenaline not given within first 5 minutes of anaphylaxis diagnosis)
critical_errors.explanation: Adrenaline is the ONLY first-line treatment for anaphylaxis - delays increase mortality risk

critical_errors.error: Wrong adrenaline route (IV instead of IM - unless cardiac arrest)
critical_errors.explanation: IV adrenaline in anaphylaxis (without cardiac arrest) can cause fatal arrhythmias - IM is standard route

critical_errors.error: Wrong adrenaline dose (prescribed 0.3mg instead of 0.5mg for adult >12 years)
critical_errors.explanation: Adult dose is 0.5mg IM (0.5mL of 1:1000), pediatric <12 years is 0.3mg

critical_errors.error: Missed anaphylaxis diagnosis (diagnosed as 'allergic reaction' without recognizing anaphylaxis criteria)
critical_errors.explanation: Anaphylaxis criteria: allergen exposure + respiratory compromise + hypotension - requires immediate adrenaline

critical_errors.error: Premature discharge (discharged before 4-6 hour observation period)
critical_errors.explanation: Biphasic reactions occur in 20% of anaphylaxis cases, typically 4-12 hours after initial reaction

critical_errors.error: Failed to prescribe EpiPen on discharge
critical_errors.explanation: All patients with anaphylaxis MUST be discharged with adrenaline auto-injector and action plan

fracp_reviews.reviewer_credentials: FACEM (Fellow Australasian College for Emergency Medicine), 16 years post-fellowship
fracp_reviews.clinical_accuracy: Excellent - classic anaphylaxis presentation with all key features (urticaria, angioedema, respiratory compromise, hypotension)
fracp_reviews.difficulty_appropriate: Yes - Medium difficulty appropriate for anaphylaxis (multiple system involvement, time-critical)
fracp_reviews.rag_citations_correct: Yes - eTG Allergy 1.3 citations verified and accurate
fracp_reviews.feedback: Excellent emergency persona. Classic anaphylaxis. Good emphasis on IM adrenaline route (critical error to give IV). Consider adding ASCIA anaphylaxis criteria (explicit diagnostic criteria) for teaching purposes.

fracp_reviews.clinical_accuracy: Accurate anaphylaxis management - correct sequence (adrenaline → oxygen → fluids → secondary treatments)
fracp_reviews.feedback: Good persona. Management sequence correct (adrenaline first-line). Excellent inclusion of biphasic reaction warning (4-6h obs). Suggest mentioning glucagon as alternative if patient on beta-blockers (theoretical consideration).

learning_objectives: Administer adrenaline 0.5mg IM as FIRST-LINE treatment (within 5 minutes)
Understand critical error: IM not IV adrenaline (unless cardiac arrest)
Apply DRSABCD framework in emergency setting
Recognize biphasic reaction risk (4-6 hour observation required)
Prescribe EpiPen and anaphylaxis action plan on discharge
